content.thinking:
I'll write the whole file in one go without testing, focusing on getting the API calls right. For the design, I'm going for an Overwatch-style chopper motorbike: bold clean shapes, dark gunmetal with white panels, and a single strong orange accent color, with realistic proportions around 2.4-2.6m length and 1.1m height.

Now I'm working out the skeleton and coordinate layout -- positioning wheels, fork rake, and joints like steering, kickstand, and levers -- then figuring out how to orient the torus-based tire geometry so its axis aligns correctly with the wheel's spin direction.

Still writing tire geometry...

Still working out spoke geometry...

I should keep part count manageable, staying around 300 total. Now I'm sketching the chopper frame: a hardtail design with a main spine tube running from the steering head down to the seat post, built from rigid cylindrical rods on the root bone, with capsule-style joins for connections. I'm plotting key points—head tube top and bottom, and the fork raking forward at roughly 40 degrees from the head down to the front axle—to define the chopper's silhouette.

Working out the fork geometry: computing the rake angle between the head tube and axle position to get an extreme chopper lean (settling around 47 degrees), then defining the steering axis direction and placing the triple-tree and fork legs as offset tubes—thin chrome stanchions up top transitioning into thicker, darker lower sliders near the axle.

Setting the front wheel, handlebars, headlight, and fender as children of a "steer" joint that pivots at the triple tree along the fork's direction vector, so they all turn together. For the handlebars I'm going with pullback chopper-style bars, sketching separate catmull-rom curves for each grip that sweep from the triple tree mount outward and up to the hand positions.

Adding chrome bar segments with black rubber grips at the tips, then setting up left/right clutch and brake lever joints hinged near the grips, carefully mirroring the X coordinates so the rider's right and left sides stay correctly oriented given how the model's local axes relate to world space.

Now I'm laying out the main frame geometry: positioning the rear axle, then sweeping the backbone top tube from the head area down to the seat, and starting the downtube from the head toward the engine mount.

Next I'm adding the rear hardtail rails connecting the seat and engine to the rear axle, then working out how to build the rear fender as a partial cylinder sweep that arcs over the tire without wrapping all the way around.

Still working out the sweep angles...

For the front fender, I'll attach it to the steer bone with a shorter arc sweeping from about 75° down to -35°, keeping the same half-width so it moves naturally with the fork. Then for the engine, I'm planning a V-twin with a crankcase box and two cylinders angled in a V shape, tilted in the side view, with stacked thin disk fins and a dark gunmetal and chrome color scheme.

Still writing cylinder geometry...

Still working out pipe coordinates...

Defining pipe geometry per side...

Checking pipe end clearance against the tire, it fits fine. Now I'm working out the teardrop gas tank shape, placing stations along the backbone with varying widths and heights to loft a tapered tank profile sitting above the frame.

I'm designing the paint scheme for the tank -- an orange base with a gray underside, plus a white racing stripe band across the top, using position and normal checks to assign colors in distinct blocks rather than gradients.

Now I'm adding a decal, like a stylized lightning bolt or emblem, placed on the tank's surface using the loft sweep as the decal target, positioning and sizing it to sit on one side and mirroring it for the other side.

I want to be careful about bone assignment for the loft stations since automatic nearest-joint selection could grab the wrong joint, so I'll explicitly set the bone to the frame joint everywhere for the tank and seat lofts. For the seat, I'm defining loft stations tapering from the back toward the front with varying width and height, planning a black leather material with orange stitched piping along the edges for contrast.

Now I'm designing a tall curved sissy bar behind the seat using a chrome sweep along a catmull-rom path that arcs up from the rear rails and loops across, with a padded section, checking that the overall height stays reasonable relative to the handlebar height.

Still writing headlight geometry...

Realizing the fork width would intersect, I'm repositioning the headlight to sit forward of the fork, settling on a mounted spot roughly at [0,0.92,0.74] with small bracket rods connecting it to the fork legs. I'm also adding a small speedo gauge near the top of the handlebars, around [0,1.11,0.46], as a cylinder with a glowing face aimed upward.

Now I'm working through the rear wheel details—sprocket, belt, and a thin brake disc near the hub—then shifting to the front wheel's tire geometry, considering whether to texture the tread using angle-based paint calculations relative to the wheel's static pose rather than adding costly extra geometry.

I'm also settling the color palette: orange rim accents against gunmetal spokes and chrome hub, keeping the whole scheme under the 64-color budget with grays, chromes, and orange as the accent tones.

For the kickstand, I'm positioning it folded up under the frame so the bike leans realistically while both wheels still touch the floor, working out the pivot point and rod angle for a tucked-away resting position.

Now I'm placing forward footpegs for the chopper, running a rod outward from the frame mount near the engine so the rider's feet sit comfortably ahead of the usual position.

I'm also building the left-side belt/primary drive: a wide crankcase box, a chromed primary cover cylinder with an orange accent ring, and a transmission housing tucked behind it.

I need to shift the belt and pulley positions since they're conflicting with the rear tire edge and swing frame rails, so I'm nudging things to x=0.15-0.17 range and placing the axle plates and rails at ±0.19-0.2 to avoid overlap.

For the frame structure, I'm routing the top rail from the backbone/seat post down through a branch point to the rear axle, and a bottom rail from the engine mount to the same axle point, checking that the belt stays clear inside the rails. Then I'm working out the rear fender's arc geometry relative to the axle and seat position, tracing its curve at different angles to make sure it clears the seat before sweeping down toward the tire.

Continuing the fender sweep, I'm calculating the end position near θ=-60/-70 degrees to place a small glowing red tail light, then figuring out where to position a license plate below it with decal text.

I'm placing the taillight and license plate near the rear fender, then checking overall bike dimensions — total length around 2.9m and height 1.25m, confirming nothing protrudes awkwardly beyond the frame.

Verifying wheel floor contact: both front and rear tires sit flush at y=0 once accounting for ring radius plus tube thickness. I'm working through torus geometry scaling to confirm the tire cross-section stays correct when stretched along its axis, then computing axle positions and checking the rotation needed to orient each torus properly as a wheel.

Now I'm setting up helper functions for building body parts, then designing a reusable `wheel()` function that assembles the tire, rim, hub, spokes, and disc for both front and back wheels. For the spokes, I'm defining their geometry as thin boxes rotated around the x-axis to fan out radially, sized relative to the rim radius.

Writing wheel geometry...

Working out the tire paint function...

I'm settling on orange for the fenders and tank, gunmetal for frame and engine, chrome pipes, with white accent stripes for color blocking. With around 150 parts now, I'm adding engine fins, bolts, and other details, then starting the joint hierarchy with a root frame joint positioned above the wheel.

For the steering and wheel joints, I need to work out axle orientation carefully -- the steer joint aims toward a target, and the front wheel should inherit that tilted orientation so its local X-axis lines up as the axle, letting it spin correctly without needing an explicit direction override.

Now I'm mapping out the full joint hierarchy: frame as root, then steer, frontWheel, rearWheel, kickstand, pegs, levers, and throttle, mostly using hinge roles, and confirming the bone/paint API types work with these joint definitions.

For the glow treatment, I'm deciding to skip a full toon/cel aesthetic since this isn't quite the right style, instead using glow selectively for the headlamp, tail light, gauge, and maybe an orange accent strip rather than overusing it everywhere. I'm about to start sketching out the SVG assets, beginning with a tank emblem design.

Designing emblem shape and plate text...

Now I'm figuring out how to place a decal on the tank surface, working out the position and direction vectors relative to the tank's width and sweep target.

To make the emblem point forward on both sides, I'll mirror the drawing on the +X side while leaving the -X side as-is, since mirroring flips the apparent direction correctly. Then I'll add the chrome tank cap cylinder at the top of the tank per the loft stations.

I'm positioning the tank cap near the top and working out the tank cross-section stations by z-coordinate, checking that the top tube and backbone curve stay clear of the tank's bottom edge at each station, adjusting for slight overlap where needed.

I'm adjusting the backbone curve to keep a small clearance gap below the tank, and adding mounting bands as dark strap lines in the paint function to simulate the metal straps wrapping the tank.

Writing tank paint function...

Defining a shade helper that mixes highlight colors based on surface normal, then working out seat paint: black leather with orange piping at the side positions (around 90° and 270° on the loft path), plus considering diamond-stitch detailing on the top surface.

Adding stitch lines, frame and engine casing paint...

Settling on an Overwatch-style color scheme: orange as the dominant color, white as secondary, with chrome accents and orange rims for a strong pop. I'll keep part count manageable by grouping small bolts into merged geometries where possible, then start writing the actual builder code.

Starting the component imports and setup...

Still defining joints...

I'm sketching helper functions for parts and rods, importing the Joint and Paint types to keep things properly typed.

Now I'm defining a wheel-building function that takes bone, position, ring/tube dimensions, rim radius, spoke length, and tire color as parameters, then constructs the tire geometry...

Still computing wheel geometry...

Adding engine detail geometry...

I'm checking the geometry math for crank and barrel positions, making sure the front head and downtube placements stay clear of the engine and backbone without overlapping.

Placing the crankcase, oil pan, and gearbox as boxes below the down tube, then adding the primary cover, bottom rails connecting to axle mount plates, and the rear axle cylinder to complete the lower frame assembly.

Still plotting pipe paths...

Placing the chrome air cleaner in the V gap near the cylinders, then adding a few extra details on the opposite side like an oil tank cylinder and small accent parts to balance the composition.

Now building the handlebar assembly: triple tree box at the steering axis, riser rods going up from the tree, then sweeping chrome tubes through control points to form the bar shape, and defining rod placements for the grips at the bar ends.

Still working out positions for the throttle hinge joint on the right grip and the clutch lever pivot on the left, aiming each lever's rod back toward the rider.

I'm considering mirrors with stems and discs at the bar ends, but the height gets too tall for the frame, so I'll just skip adding mirrors altogether.

Now I'm working out the front fork: chrome stanchions and gun-metal sliders, rubber gaiters with ridges, and a lower triple tree box, making sure the fork legs stay parallel to the steering axis by matching their top and bottom offsets to the direction vector.

I'm also placing the front fender as an arc sweeping around the tire with proper clearance, keeping it centered between the fork legs, and adding small stay rods and brackets connecting the fender to the fork sliders at a chosen angle.

Checking the arc sweep covers front-to-back of the fender correctly, then I'm sweeping the fender profile along that path with a thin box cross-section, considering adding a rim lip ridge for detail.

Now for the rear fender I'm using the same radius-sweep approach at a slightly larger radius, plus chrome edge trim rods offset along the fender's width, and a white stripe painted down the center using a position mask. I'm planning the headlight bucket via lathe geometry with a chrome rim torus and glowing lens, skipping turn signals and horn for now, and considering side panel decals for the name.

Now I'm mapping out remaining details: kickstand pivot and foot pad placement, peg joints with rubber cylinder grips and mounting boxes, and the front brake disc with slotted steel texture plus a caliper box positioned near the fork.

I'm positioning the rear brake disc on the opposite side, adding a rear pulley with belt rods connecting to the transmission sprocket, and deciding to skip extra coil-spring details for the hardtail rear suspension before moving on to the seat mount.

Adding a glowing red taillight sphere with a mounting plate beneath it, then thinking through extra finishing touches like a tank cap, speedometer, and key switch, plus working out how to orient exhaust heat-shield clamp rings along the pipe path using tangent frames from the sweep function.

Varying the pipe radius with a quadratic function of t, and using a string-based color function to create darker and chrome bands along the tube for visual segmentation, both tied to the bone. I'll skip mounting brackets but consider adding a thin glowing orange LED-style strip along the fork for accent lighting.

I'm planning small bolt loops around the primary cover, rocker covers, and axle plates using tiny cylinders, plus a glowing orange torus accent on the primary cover. Writing a tire paint function...

I verify the ring position lands correctly on the sidewall for both front and rear wheels given the elliptical scaling, so that checks out and I'll skip disc paint detailing.

Now I'm sketching the gauge SVG with a dark circular background, an orange arc gauge indicator, and tick marks around it.

Still writing gauge markup...

For the emblem, I'm designing a bolt-chevron polygon shape with a light fill and dark stroke outline, double-checking the point sequence forms a coherent arrow-like shape even though the path self-intersects slightly -- which is fine for SVG rendering purposes.

Now I'm building the license plate texture, with rounded white background, dark border, bold "CH0P-77" text, and an orange accent strip, then mapping it onto a plane geometry oriented to face backward so the text reads correctly from behind the tank, and starting to set up the decal placement parameters.

Adding more part geometry...

Positioning axle nuts and the rear axle cylinder, then laying out the steering head tube geometry and adjusting the down tube and backbone start points to connect properly.

I'm checking the tank-to-saddle and head tube alignment, setting up a rod wrapper helper, and planning glow materials for the gauge lens and lamp parts. Now I'm writing the actual geometry code carefully, watching for unused variable errors.
